subtitle: Belonging grows when work is usable, employees have real choices and colleagues see one another beyond assumptions. Learn how these pieces build meaningful participation for employees with disabilities.
scope: For staff, teams, facilitators and leaders in DSD or other DHS work areas. Original practice cases support learning and practical reflection; they do not determine disability, job qualifications, accommodation eligibility or an individual IDI position. Keep personal medical information out of learning notes and follow actual agency responsibilities. The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads the program through guidance, knowledge and feedback; staff carry their own work. Excluded Native American or Tribal-specific matters go to the person or area responsible within ADSA (Aging and Disability Services Administration).
introTranscript: Belonging involves being recognized as a colleague with meaningful work, judgment, relationships and choices. An employee with a disability should not have to become an inspirational example, disclose a private history or accept unnecessary help to be included. This course examines how assumptions can narrow opportunity, how different learned meanings of care can be understood, and how accessible work and actual support responsibilities fit together. You will practice with practice DSD decisions, review mixed results without inventing a belonging score, and consider your own understanding privately. The focus is useful participation and respect for agency, not guessing disability from appearance or deciding what another person ought to want.

lessons.title: Recognize the colleague and the actual opportunity
lessons.summary: Examine how praise and protection can become exclusion when they replace meaningful work and an employee’s own judgment.
lessons.objective: Distinguish relevant task information from an assumption about an employee with a disability.
objectives: Distinguish relevant task information from an assumption about an employee with a disability.
Identify how a seemingly supportive decision can narrow meaningful participation.
Choose a response that restores the work question and the employee’s opportunity to contribute.
takeaways: A colleague is more than an assumed limitation or an inspiring story.
An invitation needs a real task and a chance to influence it.
Examine the work and ask before treating protection as the person’s preference.
lessons.statement: Make room for the colleague’s contribution rather than defining it through your assumption.

image.caption: A shared task offers a meaningful place for a colleague’s knowledge and judgment.

intro.heading: A welcome that leaves out the work
intro.body:
In a practice DSD project, Jan joins a group revising a service explanation. Jan has relevant experience comparing complex notices. A colleague knows Jan has a disability and recommends keeping Jan away from the detailed comparison so the work will not be tiring. Instead, Jan is asked to appear in an introduction about how inclusive the team is. Nobody has asked about Jan’s interest, the proposed task or what would make it usable. A warm intention has replaced an ordinary professional opportunity with a symbolic role.

The first question is not whether the colleague meant well. It is what the decision does. Jan can examine the notices, contribute an interpretation and have the argument considered alongside other evidence. A public introduction cannot substitute for that work. Nor does information that a person has a disability establish which task they can do, which format they need or what they want to share. The project needs relevant knowledge, a clear assignment and the actual review of the contribution. It does not need a private medical story to make those matters clear.

Compare three invitations. “You can show everyone how resilient you are” defines the person through an observer’s story. “You can sit with us while others do the complicated section” provides proximity without meaningful responsibility. “We are comparing these two explanations; would you like to review the sequence, and is the material usable for that review?” opens a real contribution. It states the purpose and allows a response about the task. Actual assignment authority and any support process still belong to the appropriate roles; the invitation does not promise an unapproved change.

Belonging is not created by exempting a person from every challenge or praising every answer. Jan’s comparison can be questioned respectfully, supported by sources or revised through ordinary review. The important change is that the colleague is approached as someone whose reasoning matters. In your own reflection, notice whether you associate disability with dependency, unusual courage or an automatic need for protection. Those associations may be familiar without being an adequate account of this person. Learning begins when you recognize that gap and return to the person, the task and the available evidence.

inThisLesson: Practice a response that preserves contribution and choice.
lessons.keyStatement: Support should help a colleague participate in meaningful work, not replace that participation with a story about them.

flashcards.back: A real opportunity to contribute knowledge, judgment or work and have it considered in the task. Being present alone does not establish this.
A person’s ability to express choices and take part in decisions that concern them, within the actual work and responsibilities.
A conclusion about what a person can do that has not been established by relevant information about the task and person.
A feature of material, technology, arrangement or process that interferes with usable participation.
An employment adjustment considered through the actual agency process for a qualified applicant or employee with a disability; this course does not decide eligibility.
Visibility that presents someone as evidence of inclusion while leaving their actual contribution or influence unclear.

accordion.heading: Return from the label to the colleague

items.title: Identify the contribution
items.body: Jan’s notice-comparison experience connects directly with the project question. Explain what is being compared and how the review will use the findings. This makes the invitation understandable. A vague “join us” can still leave Jan without material, responsibility or a receiving response, so specify the work rather than rely on friendly proximity.

items.title: Examine the protection
items.body: The proposed exclusion rests on a guess about tiring work. It has not been established through Jan’s account or the actual task. Do not turn the guess into a performance finding. Ask about participation and usable material within the work arrangement, then respond through the appropriate process if an actual support need is raised.

items.title: Receive the reasoning
items.body: When Jan contributes a sequence comparison, examine the examples and explain how they affect the draft. Neither inspirational praise nor automatic agreement addresses the reasoning. A respectful challenge can belong in an inclusive review when the person has a fair opportunity to understand the question, supply evidence and respond.

tabs.heading: Compare what the invitation actually offers

tabs.label: An inspiring example
tabs.body: Jan is visible in a presentation but the detailed work is withheld. The team can claim a diverse picture while losing relevant notice knowledge. The correction is not more admiring language. Offer the actual comparison and ask about its usability, allowing Jan to choose what personal information, if any, is shared publicly.

tabs.label: Protected from all challenge
tabs.body: Avoiding difficult work might look considerate, but it assumes what Jan can manage and denies the chance to develop or demonstrate relevant reasoning. Ordinary review can remain demanding and respectful. Clarify the task and actual supports rather than decide privately that every complex assignment is inappropriate.

tabs.label: A colleague with relevant judgment
tabs.body: The invitation connects Jan’s knowledge with an open comparison, usable information and a real response. It allows questions without making gratitude or personal disclosure the entry price. The draft can still change through evidence and authorized review; meaningful participation does not mean automatic approval of any person’s preferred wording.

check.question: What best improves Jan’s practice invitation?
check.correct: Offer the relevant notice-comparison task, explain how the contribution will be considered, and ask about usable participation instead of assigning a symbolic role from a disability assumption.
wrong: Ask Jan to describe a private struggle so the group will feel inspired.
Keep Jan in the group photo while permanently withholding detailed work.
Accept every suggestion without review to show support.
check.feedbackCorrect: This restores a real professional contribution and keeps the person’s choice and reasoning in view.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A private struggle is not required for an ordinary contribution. A photo offers visibility but does not restore the withheld work. Automatic agreement also bypasses Jan’s reasoning instead of taking it seriously. Offer the real task, usable material and a receiving review.

items.text: Jan has experience comparing complex notices.
The group needs a comparison of two explanation sequences.
Jan is offered the actual draft and a way to supply reasoning.
The person responsible will explain how the comparison affected the draft.
Knowing Jan has a disability proves detailed work should be withheld.
A public resilience story replaces the opportunity to review the notice.

lessons.next: Next, examine different learned meanings of offering and receiving help.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Jan’s relevant notice-review experience is known, but a colleague proposes a ceremonial role and withholds the detailed comparison without asking about the task or usable participation.
scenario.prompt: What should the project lead do?
options: Restore the actual review opportunity, explain its purpose and receiving process, and ask about usable participation without requiring a public personal story.
Keep the ceremonial role because a friendly intention makes the choice inclusive.
Approve every future suggestion without examining its evidence.
responses: This recognizes Jan as a colleague whose contribution and choices matter.
Intention does not undo the loss of a meaningful task; the choice needs examination.
Treating the reasoning seriously involves ordinary evidence and review, not automatic agreement.

lessons.transfer: Identify the actual contribution, unsupported protection and changed invitation in the practice case. Explain what still needs ordinary review.

move.control: You can clarify an opportunity and examine an assumption before it determines someone’s role.
move.failure: A colleague becomes a symbol of inclusion while meaningful work is withheld.
move.next: Review one invitation using practice or cleared material: does it offer contribution and a receiving response, or only visibility?

lessons.title: Understand care without taking over
lessons.summary: Use individually meanings the people describe of help to move from a familiar intention toward a response that respects choice and useful support.
lessons.objective: Explain two individually supplied learned meanings of offering help in an example.
objectives: Explain two individually supplied learned meanings of offering help in an example.
Describe how each familiar meaning can misread the other person’s response.
Develop a wider response that makes assistance available while retaining the recipient’s choice.
takeaways: An offer can carry a learned meaning beyond the immediate task.
Receiving help does not have one universal meaning.
A wider response can express care while allowing a person to choose what happens.
lessons.statement: Understand the meaning of an offer and change the response without deciding for the person.

image.caption: Assistance is more useful when the offer and the person’s choice are both understood.

intro.heading: Two meanings of helping
intro.body:
In an original practice DSD encounter, Carmen sees Taylor organizing papers before a review. Carmen begins moving the papers into a pile she considers easier to reach. Taylor asks her to stop. Carmen feels the response rejects kindness; Taylor feels an ordinary work arrangement has been taken over. Looking only at the movements leaves the exchange as one person helping and another appearing ungrateful. The participants’ meanings the people describe give a fuller account.

Carmen explains that in the shared household tasks where she learned care, people noticed a burden and began helping before it had to be named. Waiting for a request could suggest that a person’s difficulty did not matter. Taylor explains learning in a different setting that a person’s arrangement should remain theirs until they invited help. Asking first communicated trust in their judgment; taking over could suggest the work was no longer regarded as theirs. These are the people in the example’ accounts. They do not define a population, diagnose a disability or establish what anyone else wants.

The first interpretations can now be reconsidered. Carmen’s action had an anticipatory care meaning, but that meaning did not establish permission to rearrange Taylor’s work. Taylor’s stop did not necessarily reject relationship or assistance; it preserved ownership of the arrangement. Both care and agency become visible in a wider frame. The useful response is more than adding “please.” Carmen can acknowledge the stop, leave the papers where Taylor wants them, and offer a specific choice: “Would moving this separate stack be useful, or would you rather keep this arrangement?” Taylor can decline, select part of the offer or explain a practical preference without defending a private history.

This example concerns an ordinary colleague offer. It does not make an actual employer support responsibility optional or replace the accommodation process. Nor does asking once create lasting permission to take over future tasks. A changed response follows the supplied meaning and the present preference. In private reflection, consider what helping means in your own learned experience. Does asking feel warm, distant, respectful or unnecessary? Recognize that your meaning can be understandable without becoming the only correct interpretation. The learning is a broader understanding of care and a more considered response, not a public test of anyone’s gratefulness.

inThisLesson: Hear the two meanings the people describe.
Develop a wider account of care and agency.
Change the actual offer and response.
lessons.keyStatement: A caring purpose becomes useful when it is understood alongside the other person’s agency and present preference.

accordion.heading: Move from familiar care toward wider understanding

items.title: Hear the anticipatory meaning
items.body: Carmen’s account explains why waiting can feel uncaring to her. That is a reason to understand the offer, not a reason to override Taylor’s stop. Keep intention and effect distinct. She can still notice a practical need and offer assistance while changing who chooses the arrangement.

items.title: Hear the ownership meaning
items.body: Taylor’s account explains why uninvited rearrangement can feel like a loss of trust. The explanation does not make all offers disrespectful or require a private disability account. Carmen can ask about the present task, and Taylor can respond to the specific offer rather than accept or reject every form of help at once.

items.title: Make the changed response visible
items.body: Carmen stops, acknowledges the arrangement and offers a bounded choice. This follows the wider meaning into actual action: care is available and the work remains Taylor’s. A polite tone without stopping would preserve the original takeover. Check what the person chooses instead of treating the new question as ceremonial.

tabs.heading: Compare three ways care can operate

tabs.label: Help before a choice
tabs.body: Carmen expresses the care she learned by moving the papers. If she keeps moving them after the stop, her intention becomes the deciding standard. The practical consequence is loss of Taylor’s arrangement. Notice a possible need, but offer assistance in a way that allows the actual recipient’s response to change what happens.

tabs.label: Never offer assistance
tabs.body: Withdrawing every offer avoids one kind of takeover but can create distance and leave practical help unavailable. Taylor’s preference in this exchange does not establish a rule that assistance is always unwelcome. Offer a specific option without pressure, and take the answer seriously rather than making a declined offer end the relationship.

tabs.label: Care with agency
tabs.body: Carmen recognizes her familiar meaning and Taylor’s different account, then changes the action. She leaves the arrangement intact and offers a specific useful option. Taylor can choose. This is a wider practice developed from individual meanings, not a guess based on disability, appearance or a supposed cultural rule for either person.

check.question: Which response follows the wider understanding in Carmen and Taylor’s practice exchange?
check.correct: Stop rearranging, acknowledge Taylor’s chosen arrangement and offer a specific optional form of help whose answer will determine what happens.
wrong: Continue moving the papers because Carmen’s kind intention establishes permission.
Require Taylor to describe a disability before honoring the stop.
Avoid every future offer because declining this help proves help is always unwanted.
check.feedbackCorrect: The action changes through the wider interpretation: care remains available and the person’s present choice matters.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Kind intention does not establish permission to continue after the stop. Respecting the arrangement does not require a disability explanation. A present decline does not establish every future preference. Stop, offer a bounded choice and allow the response to change the action.

sorting.heading: Trace meaning into an actual response

items.text: Carmen learned that noticing and helping early expressed care.
Taylor learned that asking first expressed trust in the person’s judgment.
Carmen stops and offers a specific choice without pressure.
The selected help leaves Taylor’s chosen arrangement intact.
Taylor’s stop proves private ingratitude.
An assumed disability gives a colleague permission to take over.

lessons.next: Next, examine access in the actual material and activity rather than in assumptions about the person.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Carmen’s anticipatory-care meaning and Taylor’s ask-first meaning have both been supplied. Carmen continues rearranging the papers while saying she only wants to help.
scenario.prompt: What would make the wider understanding affect the work?
options: Tell Taylor that care requires accepting the rearrangement.
Stop, acknowledge the chosen arrangement and offer a specific option that Taylor can accept, change or decline.
Treat a single declined offer as proof that every assistance option is unnecessary.
responses: This makes Carmen’s familiar meaning the only standard and preserves the takeover.
The response puts care and agency into the actual arrangement rather than merely changing the tone.
The present choice does not determine every support need or preference.

lessons.transfer: Explain the two learned meanings, both first misreadings and how the changed offer follows a wider interpretation. Do not turn either person into a group rule.

move.control: You can recognize a familiar care meaning and allow the other person’s response to change your action.
move.failure: Kind intention becomes a reason to override a person’s ordinary work choice.
move.next: Privately examine one meaning you attach to helping; practice a specific offer whose answer you would actually honor.

lessons.title: Make the contribution usable
lessons.summary: Examine the full work activity, including information, technology and response, so access is not reduced to physical presence.
lessons.objective: Identify a barrier in the material or response method of a practice task.
objectives: Identify a barrier in the material or response method of a practice task.
Distinguish a usable contribution from an arrangement that shifts the task to someone else.
Choose a material and activity improvement while retaining actual digital accessibility responsibilities.
takeaways: Presence does not establish access to the task.
Usable information and a workable response both matter.
Changing a barrier should preserve the employee’s substantive contribution.
lessons.statement: Review what the work asks a person to use, do and contribute.

image.caption: A workable review includes usable material and a way to express the person’s own reasoning.

intro.heading: The room is available; the comparison is not
intro.body:
A practice DSD group prepares an employee-development discussion about two process options. Dev can join the meeting, but the comparison appears only as an image of a table on a shared screen. The presenter names cells by color and asks for immediate reactions. Dev says the material is not usable with the reading method they use. A colleague proposes that someone else pick an option for Dev so the agenda can move on. That shortcut keeps Dev nominally present while transferring the substantive judgment to another person.

Map the task instead. Dev needs to understand the same options, inspect relevant differences and provide a reason that can affect the discussion. The group can supply a usable version of the comparison, name the options and differences clearly, and provide an opportunity to respond after reviewing it. The appropriate actual arrangements depend on the task and access process; this practice sequence is not a universal prescription for every employee. The point is that the contribution remains Dev’s, supported by usable information rather than replaced with an assumed substitute.

Consider the path before, during and after the meeting. Advance material can reveal a problem before the discussion closes. During the discussion, references such as “the green one” can still obscure the argument even when a file is available. Afterward, a response channel needs a receiver who will consider Dev’s reasoning while the choice remains open. These are connected parts of the activity. Providing one file does not by itself establish the full task is usable or that the response can influence anything.

The Minnesota State Digital Accessibility Standard applies to covered state information and communication technology, including internal work. Agencies and staff have responsibilities for creating, modifying or procuring it. Its exceptions require the actual process; convenience does not establish one. This course does not certify a document or approve an exception. In the practice case, the staff should address the current participation barrier and carry the material through the applicable accessibility work rather than call exclusion an accommodation. An individual support arrangement and accessible shared material can work together. Neither is a reason to stop examining what the actual task makes possible.

inThisLesson: Connect the improvement with actual accessibility work.
lessons.keyStatement: Access helps the person supply their own relevant reasoning rather than lets the group speak for them.

accordion.heading: Review the activity as a complete task

items.title: Information before the choice
items.body: Dev needs the options and reasons before being expected to compare them. A usable version can reduce dependence on a fast screen description. Explain which material is current and what question the review addresses. Sending several unexplained attachments can still obscure the task, even if each file is technically accessible.

items.title: Communication during the comparison
items.body: Refer to the content and meaning of a difference instead of only its color or screen position. The presenter can identify the option and explain the relationship being discussed. This helps the group examine the argument. It does not permit guessing which reading method Dev should use or treating access as someone else choosing the answer.

items.title: A response that can matter
items.body: Confirm where Dev’s comparison will be received and when it can affect the open choice. A later comment box does little if the choice closes before it is read. Keep the contribution’s substance and the receiving responsibility explicit, rather than call a passive copy of the final decision participation.

tabs.label: Another person picks
tabs.body: This saves agenda time but replaces Dev’s interpretation with someone else’s choice. It may hide a useful question about the options. Help can support reading or communication when appropriately arranged; it should not silently transfer the employee’s judgment. Ask what would make the actual comparison usable instead of assigning a proxy answer.

tabs.label: A file without a response
tabs.body: A usable document is valuable, but a decision made before Dev can respond leaves the practical opportunity incomplete. Review the schedule and receiving role as well as the file. The actual question is whether the person can use the relevant information and contribute while the choice remains meaningful.

tabs.label: Usable work and a receiving review
tabs.body: The group addresses the material, explains the differences and makes the response workable. Dev retains the comparison, and the person responsible considers its reasons. Actual accessibility and support responsibilities continue. This is a practical improvement to an activity, not proof that every barrier for every employee has disappeared.

check.question: Which adjustment best preserves Dev’s practice contribution?
check.correct: Provide usable comparison material and a workable opportunity for Dev’s own reasoning to be considered before the choice closes, while following actual accessibility responsibilities.
wrong: Have another colleague choose for Dev because both attended the same meeting.
Send a usable file only after the final choice and call that equal influence.
Label the inaccessible table an exception solely because revising it is inconvenient.
check.feedbackCorrect: The adjustment preserves the substantive comparison, usable participation and a real receiving response.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Attendance does not authorize someone else to replace Dev’s judgment. A file after the decision can inform but cannot influence that closed choice. Inconvenience does not itself establish an accessibility exception. Address the material, task timing and actual process together.

sorting.heading: Place each part of the usable contribution

items.text: The current options are supplied in a usable form.
The presenter describes an option’s meaning rather than only its color.
Dev can submit the comparison before the choice closes.
The person responsible explains how Dev’s reasoning affected the open choice.
A colleague selects for Dev without a chosen arrangement.
The final choice is copied to Dev as proof of earlier influence.

lessons.next: Next, distinguish a supportive work conversation from the actual accommodation process.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Dev can attend, but the image-only option table and color references are not usable. The group proposes having another employee choose for Dev and moving directly to the final decision.
options: Treat physical attendance as proof the task was accessible.
Have another employee choose and congratulate Dev for attending.
Address the material and communication barrier, preserve Dev’s own comparison and provide a receiving opportunity while the choice remains open.
responses: Being in the room does not establish usable information or a meaningful response.
This shifts the substantive judgment instead of making it possible for Dev.
The correction connects usable material with the employee’s own reasoning and actual influence.

lessons.transfer: Map the comparison’s information, activity, response and receiving role. Explain why a proxy answer or a later final copy does not restore the original opportunity.

move.control: You can examine a task’s actual material, language and receiving arrangement.
move.failure: The group preserves the appearance of participation while transferring the person’s judgment.
move.next: Review a practice or cleared activity from material through response; identify one barrier and the role that can address it.

lessons.title: Respond to a support request with the right process
lessons.summary: Keep a useful work conversation and the actual accommodation responsibilities connected without turning support into public medical disclosure.
lessons.objective: Recognize an initial accommodation request in an employee in this example communication.
objectives: Recognize an initial accommodation request in an employee in this example communication.
Identify the receiving role’s actual first response without inventing approval authority.
Distinguish task information useful to colleagues from medical information that belongs in the appropriate process.
takeaways: An employee does not need special words for the initial request.
A friendly work conversation does not replace the actual support process.
Colleagues need usable task arrangements, not a public medical history.
lessons.statement: Recognize the request, carry it to the right decision-maker and keep the work discussion focused.

image.caption: A support request needs an actual receiving response and careful handling of information.

intro.heading: A clear request is treated as an informal suggestion
intro.body:
In a practice DSD work discussion, Ruth tells supervisor Ellis that a medical condition makes the long live-only training session difficult and asks for a change. Ruth does not name the ADA, supply a formal diagnosis to the group or use the phrase reasonable accommodation. Ellis replies that the team values belonging and asks Ruth to share the full medical history at the next meeting so everyone will understand. The response offers reassurance while failing to recognize the actual request and exposing information the team does not need.

MMB Policy 1433 allows an initial request in any manner without special words. The recipient must promptly forward it to the appropriate decision-maker and tell the requester who that is. Where medical documentation is appropriate, the agency ADA Coordinator handles it; supervisors and managers must not request it themselves. These responsibilities belong to the actual process. A course exercise or colleague’s preferred solution does not approve or deny an accommodation.

The work conversation can remain practical. What activity is involved, what barrier has been described and how will the actual response be communicated? Ellis can recognize Ruth’s request, follow the receiving responsibility and keep the group’s discussion to the work arrangement it needs to use. The colleagues do not need to assess Ruth’s diagnosis or decide whether the request is sufficiently persuasive. Nor should a welcoming tone become a reason to leave the request in an informal suggestion pile.

Consider the information boundary. The group may need to know how to arrange the activity and who receives a follow-up question. That is different from knowing the employee’s medical history. Ruth can express a preference or ask about the process without agreeing to a public explanation. The real decision-maker may need relevant information through the proper route, so privacy here does not mean no information may ever be requested. It means the learning group and ordinary colleagues are not substituted for that route.

In the practice case, the next useful action is to carry the request correctly and make the receiving response clear. The team can also examine whether its training arrangement unnecessarily relies on one live-only method. That examination helps future work but does not erase the current request. Both can proceed: actual support for this employee and a considered review of the shared activity. Belonging becomes credible when the response connects words with the appropriate action.

inThisLesson: Separate work arrangement from medical history.
Preserve current support while improving the shared activity.
lessons.keyStatement: A recognized request should enter the actual process; it does not need a public medical story to count as a request.

accordion.heading: Connect support and the work conversation

items.title: Recognize what was communicated
items.body: Ruth connects a medical condition with a need to change the training arrangement. The lack of a legal phrase does not turn that communication into a casual idea. Ellis should act on the request through the actual receiving responsibility. Do not make the employee repeat a private explanation for a team audience before it moves forward.

items.title: Keep authority visible
items.body: The receiving response tells Ruth who will consider the request and carries it to that role. Ellis’s welcome does not establish authority to approve every possible option. A clear connection is more useful than promising an unreviewed solution or saying someone else will eventually handle it without actually forwarding the request.

items.title: Use information for its purpose
items.body: The team can discuss the training arrangement it is responsible for using. Medical documentation belongs in the proper process where appropriate, rather than in a learning exercise or group meeting. This distinction allows practical coordination without treating a colleague’s private history as the explanation everyone must receive.

tabs.label: Reassurance without action
tabs.body: Ellis says the team is inclusive and leaves Ruth’s request in a casual discussion. The person receives positive language but no actual connection to the support process. Recognize the communicated need and carry the receiving responsibility through; a welcoming sentence is valuable only alongside the appropriate response.

tabs.label: A public proof requirement
tabs.body: Asking for a group medical history makes colleagues the audience for information they do not need. It also creates an extra step before the request moves forward. Keep the work discussion practical and use the actual documentation process where appropriate, instead of making public disclosure the price of being heard.

tabs.label: The right route and a practical conversation
tabs.body: Ellis recognizes the request, follows the forwarding and notification responsibility, and keeps the team focused on the usable training arrangement. That preserves action and careful information handling. It does not promise a particular approved outcome; it makes the real receiving process and present work question clear.

check.question: How should Ellis first respond to Ruth’s practice communication?
check.correct: Recognize the request without requiring special words, promptly forward it to the appropriate decision-maker, tell Ruth who that is and keep a public medical history out of the group discussion.
wrong: Wait until Ruth uses the exact phrase reasonable accommodation.
Ask the team to judge Ruth’s full medical history before forwarding anything.
Promise that Ellis can approve every requested option without checking actual authority.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response follows the actual receiving responsibility and preserves the information boundary.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The initial request does not require special words. A team medical review is not the proper receiving or documentation process. A promise beyond actual authority can mislead Ruth about the outcome. Recognize the communication, connect the right decision-maker and keep the work discussion practical.

items.text: The request is promptly forwarded to the appropriate decision-maker.
Ruth is told who will consider the request.
Colleagues know how the approved training arrangement will operate.
The team reviews whether its shared activity unnecessarily depends on one method.
A public medical story is required before the request is forwarded.
An ordinary colleague decides eligibility from a course exercise.

lessons.next: Next, examine relationships, choice and the actual response to exclusion.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Ruth asks supervisor Ellis to change a long live-only session because of a medical condition. Ellis treats the request as casual feedback and proposes a public medical explanation.
options: Recognize and carry the request through the actual receiving process, name the decision-maker to Ruth and keep the group conversation focused on the work arrangement.
Hold the request until Ruth gives a medical presentation to colleagues.
Treat an inclusive welcome as a substitute for forwarding the request.
responses: This connects the communicated need with actual action and careful handling rather than an extra public proof step.
A group medical presentation is not required to make the initial request and misplaces information.
Positive words do not fulfill the receiving responsibility or identify who will act.

lessons.transfer: Identify what makes Ruth’s communication a request, the actual receiving action and the difference between work arrangement information and a medical history.

move.control: You can recognize a communicated support need and use the actual receiving responsibility.
move.failure: Reassurance or an extra public proof step delays an actual request.
move.next: Locate the actual agency process for your role using the source reference, without recording a colleague’s medical details in learning notes.

lessons.title: Build relationships without making someone a symbol
lessons.summary: Offer ordinary connection and meaningful choice while keeping disability disclosure, representation and formal concern responsibilities distinct.
lessons.objective: Identify a practice relationship invitation that pressures disclosure or symbolic representation.
objectives: Identify a practice relationship invitation that pressures disclosure or symbolic representation.
Revise the invitation so connection and relevant contribution do not depend on a private story.
Select the actual manager reporting response when the case includes protected-class harassment or discrimination.
takeaways: A colleague can belong without speaking for all employees with disabilities.
Relationship invitations should not require a private story or public gratitude.
A formal concern needs its actual response, not only a friendly conversation.
lessons.statement: Invite the colleague into a relationship rather than assign them an identity performance.

image.caption: Ordinary connection respects the person’s choices and the substance of the relationship.

intro.heading: An invitation becomes a representation assignment
intro.body:
In a practice DSD team, Blake is invited to an informal introduction because a colleague thinks Blake would be an inspiring spokesperson for employees with disabilities. Blake had offered to explain a useful way to compare two service examples, not to describe a private life or represent everyone with a disability. The organizer says the introduction will help others feel comfortable and that declining might seem unsupportive. An invitation has become a pressure to perform a role Blake did not choose.

Begin with the actual relationship. Colleagues can welcome Blake’s proposed comparison, ask about an interest or explain an open activity. None requires treating Blake as a spokesperson. A person’s willingness to discuss one example does not authorize a public identity story or establish the views of a group. Nor does declining a social introduction show whether the employee values the team. The relevant question is what invitation was offered, whether it is usable and whether the person’s response can actually change what happens.

Choosing to disclose and making a practical support request are also different. MMB’s Work Culture resource recognizes the employee’s choice about disability-status disclosure. That choice should not be turned into a belonging test. Actual support responsibilities continue when relevant needs are communicated. Similarly, an employer-sponsored activity is not automatically outside accommodation responsibilities merely because it is social; the EEOC guidance includes benefits and privileges of employment. Refer an actual need through the appropriate process rather than assume that optional attendance makes access irrelevant.

Now add a distinct concern to the practice case. A participant makes degrading remarks about disability, and supervisor Dana learns of the incident. Under Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report all allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination to Human Resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency procedures. A friendly conversation does not replace that duty. Dana can also address the immediate work interaction appropriately, but should not promise that a welcoming discussion settles the formal matter or that everyone must meet together.

The relational learning remains useful. Invite Blake’s actual contribution, remove pressure to disclose, receive a declined invitation without a loyalty judgment and avoid asking one person to represent a population. Those practices make ordinary connection less burdensome. Where a formal concern is present, carry the actual responsibility too. Respect is not credible when its meaning depends on a person accepting an unwanted public role.

inThisLesson: Recognize the specific manager reporting duty.
lessons.keyStatement: Connection can be offered without turning disability into a public role, while actual support and concern responsibilities remain.

accordion.heading: Keep the relationship and the roles clear

items.title: Receive the contribution that was offered
items.body: Blake proposed a comparison method. Ask about that method and how it could help the team rather than replacing it with an inspirational introduction. If Blake chooses a separate story, consider it on its own terms and appropriate sharing. A professional contribution is not implied permission to tell or request a private history.

items.title: Allow the invitation to be declined
items.body: An ordinary optional introduction can remain available without a judgment about commitment. Receiving a decline respectfully protects the relationship. It does not settle every access or support issue: if an actual need is communicated, address the relevant process rather than infer that avoiding one activity means all needs are resolved.

items.title: Respond to the actual concern
items.body: Dana’s supervisor role matters when protected-class conduct is known. Carry the immediate reporting duty instead of asking Blake to accept a group repair as the only response. Keep the learning question focused on the invitation and role boundaries; it is not an exercise in deciding whether a real allegation has been proved.

tabs.label: A spokesperson by assignment
tabs.body: The organizer takes Blake’s identity as a reason to speak for others. This can obscure Blake’s chosen comparison and create pressure to explain private experience. Restore the actual contribution and let Blake choose a separate invitation. No individual account establishes what every employee with a disability believes or needs.

tabs.label: A social activity without access attention
tabs.body: The organizer says nobody has to attend and therefore ignores a communicated access need. Choice about attendance and access to an employer-sponsored activity are separate questions. Preserve the invitation’s optional character, but carry an actual support need through the appropriate process rather than use optional attendance as a shortcut.

tabs.label: Connection and actual responsibility
tabs.body: The team welcomes the comparison, avoids an identity performance and receives a decline without a loyalty judgment. Dana carries the formal reporting responsibility when the distinct protected-class concern is known. A relationship remains possible without making Blake’s public story, gratitude or group reconciliation the condition for participation.

check.question: Which response best fits Blake’s practice invitation and Dana’s supervisor role?
check.correct: Welcome Blake’s chosen contribution without a spokesperson or disclosure requirement, and have Dana immediately report the known protected-class concern through Policy 1436’s manager route.
wrong: Make Blake explain a private disability history to prove support for the team.
Assume one employee’s view establishes the experience of everyone with a disability.
Use a friendly group conversation as a substitute for Dana’s immediate reporting duty.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response separates chosen contribution, private disclosure and the actual supervisor responsibility.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A private history is not a loyalty test. One person’s account does not represent every employee with a disability. A friendly conversation does not replace Dana’s immediate manager reporting duty for the distinct protected-class concern. Keep the invitation meaningful and carry the actual responsibility.

sorting.heading: Distinguish the invitation from the obligation

items.text: Blake’s proposed comparison is received on its merits.
An optional introduction can be declined without a loyalty judgment.
Dana immediately reports the known protected-class concern to Human Resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer.
Dana does not substitute a group discussion for the reporting responsibility.
Blake must publicly describe a private history to support the team.
A single account establishes every employee’s disability experience.

lessons.next: Finally, review what changed and what is still unknown without turning belonging into a personal score.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Blake offered a useful service-example comparison but is pressured into an inspiring disability-spokesperson role. Supervisor Dana also learns of a participant’s degrading disability remarks.
scenario.prompt: Which response keeps the relationship and actual roles clear?
options: Make a public story the condition for receiving Blake’s comparison.
Receive the proposed contribution without representation pressure and carry Dana’s immediate formal reporting responsibility for the separate concern.
Ask Blake to represent all employees with disabilities and accept a group repair as the only response.
responses: This imposes an extra personal performance instead of considering the contribution.
The response preserves choice and substantive participation while retaining the actual supervisor duty.
An individual cannot be assigned everyone’s perspective, and an informal repair cannot replace the reporting duty.

lessons.transfer: Describe the offered contribution, imposed identity role and separate supervisor obligation. Explain why declining an introduction that is not required does not establish private disloyalty.

move.control: You can make an invitation specific, receive a choice respectfully and keep actual responsibilities clear.
move.failure: Connection becomes conditional on identity performance or an unwanted public explanation.
move.next: Review one practice invitation: remove a spokesperson assumption or disclosure pressure while preserving the meaningful contribution and actual response.

lessons.title: Review progress without deciding someone’s private belonging
lessons.summary: Read observed participation, supplied experience and unfinished work together, using a specific next response rather than an employee score.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an observed work change, a supplied personal account and missing information in a practice review.
objectives: Distinguish an observed work change, a supplied personal account and missing information in a practice review.
Identify an unresolved participation barrier or receiving response without declaring overall success.
Choose a specific next action and private learning reflection that do not create an employee belonging or IDI label.
takeaways: A task improvement can matter without proving everyone feels included.
The person’s supplied account has meaning but does not stand for everyone.
Use mixed evidence to continue useful work and widen your own understanding.
lessons.statement: Review the change faithfully and keep the unfinished work visible.

image.caption: A useful review names what changed, what people actually said and what still needs a response.

intro.heading: One improvement does not tell the whole story
intro.body:
The practice DSD project revisits its participation arrangements. Jan completed a notice comparison, and the person responsible changed one sequence based on its reasoning. Dev received a usable comparison and submitted a question before the choice closed, but the response to that question is still pending. Taylor says the new ask-first offer was helpful in that exchange. The group has no supplied account from several other employees. A project summary nevertheless proposes saying that all employees with disabilities now feel fully included.

Separate the evidence. The changed notice sequence establishes a specific use of Jan’s contribution. Dev’s submitted question establishes a workable contribution path in that task, not a completed receiving response. Taylor’s supplied experience is meaningful information about that exchange, not a universal preference or a measure of everyone’s belonging. For the other employees, the relevant experience is unknown. Missing accounts should not be translated into satisfaction, absence of concern or a need to require disclosure.

A more useful review names both the improvements and the unfinished responsibility. The person responsible can finish the response to Dev’s question, retain the material improvement in the next comparison and ask an appropriately bounded question about the activity when feedback is useful. Do not require employees with disabilities to supply personal reassurance so the project can announce success. The next question could concern whether the comparison was usable or whether a submitted contribution received an answer; it does not need to ask people to defend a private identity or certify the team’s goodness.

Private learning can accompany the work. You might notice that you initially read a declined offer as ungratefulness, then understood the agency meaning in Taylor’s account. Record that change as your own reflection if you choose, without recording Taylor as an IDI position or a personality type. Personal understanding has value even when it does not produce a public score. A task result and intrinsic learning are related possibilities, not competing tests of whose growth matters.

Follow-through should stay specific. Who will answer Dev’s question? What information does that role need, and when will the next actual update occur? Which material change is retained, and where is its use checked? These are practical review questions, not promises of universal belonging or retention. A faithful mixed account can recognize genuine progress while preserving the remaining work. That is stronger than a confident conclusion unsupported by the people and evidence available.

inThisLesson: Separate change, account and unknown information.
Choose a useful next review action.
Reflect privately without labeling the employee.
lessons.keyStatement: A faithful review can recognize progress and preserve uncertainty without demanding personal reassurance.

accordion.heading: Keep three kinds of evidence distinct

items.title: Observed work change
items.body: Jan’s comparison affected the notice sequence. Name the contribution and what changed, with appropriate handling of actual material. This shows use in that task. It does not establish every employee’s experience, the removal of every barrier or a permanent effect on retention. Keep the conclusion proportionate to the observed change.

items.title: Supplied experience
items.body: Taylor’s helpful-offer account gives meaning to that exchange and can guide the next ordinary offer. Do not turn it into a rule about every employee with a disability or lasting permission to take over. Receive the account as supplied, and ask about the present arrangement when the next situation requires a choice.

items.title: Unfinished or missing information
items.body: Dev’s question remains pending and other experiences are unknown. Preserve both rather than average them into a success claim. Assign the receiving response and keep an appropriate feedback opportunity available. An absent account does not justify a public disclosure requirement or establish that a private concern does not exist.

tabs.label: Complete belonging from one success
tabs.body: The summary uses Jan’s meaningful contribution to claim everyone feels included. It stretches task evidence into a private population-wide conclusion. Recognize what the comparison changed, but retain Dev’s pending answer and the unknown experiences. Progress can be stated accurately without making it universal.

tabs.label: No value until every account is known
tabs.body: Withholding recognition until everyone reports a feeling misses the real task improvement and can pressure people to disclose. Describe the observed change and Taylor’s supplied account while naming the limits. The next practical response does not need a complete inventory of private experience to be useful.

tabs.label: Specific progress and continuing work
tabs.body: The review records the changed sequence, usable comparison, helpful offer and pending response separately. It assigns Dev’s answer and retains the material improvement, while leaving unsupplied experiences unknown. This supports useful follow-through and personal learning without converting disability, belonging or IDI assumptions into employee data.

check.question: What is the strongest summary of the practice review?
check.correct: The notice comparison affected one sequence, the usable material enabled Dev’s question whose answer remains pending, and Taylor reported one helpful exchange; other experiences are unknown and the next response should be assigned.
wrong: One changed sequence proves that all employees with disabilities now feel included.
No improvement may be acknowledged until every employee supplies a personal account.
No feedback from several employees proves that they have no concerns.
check.feedbackCorrect: The summary keeps observed change, supplied experience, missing information and unfinished response distinct.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One task result cannot establish everyone’s private belonging. Requiring every personal account pressures disclosure and prevents recognition of known progress. Missing feedback does not establish absence of concern. State the supported change and carry the unfinished response without a personal score.

sorting.heading: Read the review without filling in the gaps

items.text: Jan’s reasoning affected one notice sequence.
Dev submitted the comparison question before the decision closed.
Taylor said the specific ask-first offer was helpful.
An employee described the revised comparison as usable in that task.
The answer to Dev’s question is still pending.
Several employees have not supplied an account of their experience.

lessons.next: Use the job aid on a practice or appropriately cleared work activity and keep private learning separate from employee data.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: One notice sequence changed through Jan’s reasoning, Dev’s timely question remains unanswered and Taylor reported a helpful offer. Several other experiences are unknown. The proposed summary says all employees with disabilities feel included.
scenario.prompt: What should the person responsible do?
options: Publish the universal claim because the project needs a clear success story.
Require every employee to disclose a private experience before acknowledging any improvement.
Report the specific changes and supplied account with their limits, assign the pending answer and keep other experiences unknown without a belonging score.
responses: The clear story exceeds the available evidence and erases unfinished work.
Personal disclosure is not required to recognize known progress or assign the next response.
This keeps progress, uncertainty and actual follow-through visible without labeling employees.

lessons.transfer: Write a brief practice review separating observed work change, supplied experience and unfinished information. Add one next response and, if useful, one private reflection about your own assumptions.

move.control: You can state a supported conclusion and carry a specific unfinished responsibility.
move.failure: A task success becomes a private employee score or a universal claim of belonging.
move.next: Choose one unfinished receiving response from a practice review and identify who can act, what information is needed and the next actual update.

jobAid.subtitle: A practical review of contribution, choice, access and follow-through.
remember: Recognize the colleague, examine the actual task, keep choices meaningful and carry real support responsibilities through the appropriate process.

sections.heading: Recognize the colleague
items: Name the actual work opportunity and relevant contribution rather than a guessed limitation or inspirational role.
Examine whether protection, praise or visibility has replaced meaningful participation.
Offer a specific invitation whose response can affect what happens.

sections.heading: Understand and respond
items: Hear individually meanings the people describe of help and agency without creating a population rule.
Develop a wider interpretation, then change the actual offer or arrangement.
Make material, activity and the receiving response usable while preserving the person’s own reasoning.

sections.heading: Carry the actual responsibilities
items: Recognize a communicated support request and use the actual agency receiving process; keep group discussion focused on work arrangements.

Where a manager or supervisor becomes aware of an allegation or incident of protected-class harassment or discrimination, carry Policy 1436’s immediate Human Resources or agency Affirmative Action Officer reporting duty and follow agency procedures.
Learning, a friendly discussion or a symbolic role does not settle an actual support or formal concern responsibility.

sections.heading: Review faithfully
items: Separate observed work changes, supplied experience, pending responses and unknown information.
Assign the unfinished response and retain useful material changes without declaring universal belonging or retention.
Private reflection can remain your own; do not turn another employee into a belonging, personality or IDI record.

sources.title: Minnesota IT Services — State Digital Accessibility Standard

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Work Culture

sources.note: Federal guidance supplies the limited benefits-and-privileges distinction, including employer-sponsored activities; whether attendance is required does not by itself determine actual accommodation responsibilities. Minnesota process applies to the course work cases.

sources.note: Current actual manager and supervisor reporting responsibility applies to the separate protected-class concern in lesson five. Informal connection does not replace the formal process.
